To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the mobility of a tagged particle in an asymmetric simple exclusion system is not equal to its self-diffusion coefficient; (ii) the mobility is given by a formula that involves the Green’s function of the system, and is thus computable in principle.
(1) The mobility for a tagged particle can be computed in a general setting of a diffusive, nonreversible, interacting particle systems with an external field.
(i) the mobility is not equal to the diffusion matrix, and that (ii) the mobility can be computed using the same method that we use to prove the Einstein relation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: 1) What is the mobility of a tagged particle in a simple exclusion system with an asymmetric jump rate? 2) Is the mobility equal to the diffusion matrix in equilibrium?
the following question: what is the mobility of a tagged particle in a non-reversible asymmetric exclusion system in d ⩾3?

the following questions: (1) How does the tracer particle move in the presence of a weak external field, (2) How does this velocity depend on the strength and the direction of the external field, (3) How does this mobility relate to the self-diffusivity in the equilibrium case?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mobility is not equal to the self-diffusivity for all asymmetric mean zero random walks with simple exclusion.
the mobility of a tracer particle does not coincide with the self-difusion matrix of the particle in equilibrium for all asymmetric mean-zero random walk models.
the mobility is the sum of two contributions: one is the equilibrium self-diffusion, and the other is a correction term that is not related to equilibrium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that for any mean zero asymmetric simple random walk, the Einstein relation fails to hold.
we show how to calculate the mobility for a tagged particle when the system is in a non-equilibrium steady state.
the Einstein relation holds for diffusive systems with a finite number of particles, but fails to hold for systems with an infinite number of particles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the presence of an external field, the tracer particle in a non-reversible system behaves very differently compared to that in a reversible system.
the mobility of a tagged particle in an asymmetric exclusion system can be expressed in terms of the current of tagged particle in equilibrium.
the Einstein relation fails to hold when the perturbation is not symmetric in space.
